stories.headline: Nepal flash floods LIVE: Death toll rises to 675; India sends tunnel rescue team to Nepal
stories.deck: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the government is with the flood-affected citizens of the country and its priority is to save the life of every citizen
stories.bodyText:
The death toll from flash floods in Nepal rose to 675 on Saturday (August 29, 2026), with bodies continuing to be recovered as search and rescue operations pressed ahead amid renewed rainfall, rising water levels and fears of further flooding in the Bhotekoshi River basin.
Nearly 2,400 people remained missing, including at least 320 foreign nationals, while more than 4,400 people have been rescued or evacuated so far as rescuers race against time to reach remote settlements cut off by the destruction of roads and bridges.
Also read | A shared disaster, beyond borders and geopolitics
Nepal’s Foreign Minister and the UN climate chief warned of the growing threat from global warming to the Himalayas, as rescuers race to find thousands missing after torrential flooding along the border with China.

stories.headline: World Liberty Financial | Trump’s crypto U-turn
stories.deck: Investments from a top UAE official into U.S. President’s crypto enterprise attract criticisms of conflict of interest and foreign influence
stories.bodyText:
U.S. President Donald Trump has built a business empire spanning real estate, casinos and entertainment. His family’s growing crypto dealings are now facing mounting criticism over conflicts of interest and foreign influence.
A top United Arab Emirates official holds a stake in the family’s latest venture: a planned crypto bank now drawing scrutiny over foreign ties to a sitting President. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed al Nahyan, the UAE’s national security adviser, and his co-investors own a major stake in the company behind that bank.
Earlier this month, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency gave conditional approval to World Liberty Financial, backed by Mr. Trump’s family and close allies, to set up a federally chartered U.S. trust bank to issue, redeem and safeguard a dollar-backed stablecoin, USD1.
Mr. Tahnoon and his co-investors own a 49% stake in the bank’s holding company, the Journal reported. “The shareholder structure of the bank’s holding company, called WLTC Holdings, is the same as World Liberty’s, though Tahnoon and his co-investors used a different entity — called StringZ Holding RSC — for the stake in WLTC. An entity affiliated with the Trump family holds a 38% stake,” the Journal said, quoting a source.
Mr. Tahnoon and others had invested $500 million in World Liberty Financial in January 2025. “The deal, signed four days before President Trump’s inauguration, steered $263 million to Trump family entities, according to the President’s most recent financial disclosure,” the Journal noted.
A stablecoin is designed to maintain a stable value and reduce volatility. It is pegged to a currency, commodity or other asset, which may be held in reserve to back its value.
“USD1 now has a market value of $4 billion. World Liberty says the dollars backing USD1 are invested in U.S. Treasury and other cash equivalents, generating an estimated $150 million a year in interest,” the Journal reported.
Mr. Trump was not always fond of cryptocurrencies. During his first term, he bashed Facebook’s plans to create a digital currency. He dismissed Bitcoin and its peers as “not money,” calling their value “highly volatile and based on thin air”. In 2021, he told Fox Business that Bitcoin was a “scam”. “I think they should regulate them very, very high,” he said, adding, “It takes the edge off of the dollar and the importance of the dollar.”
Policy shift
That changed as the 2024 election approached. Crypto companies funnelled more than $119 million into a non-partisan super PAC to elect pro-crypto candidates in that cycle, and Mr. Trump vowed to make the United States the “crypto capital of the planet”.
In March 2025, Mr. Trump created the U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve by executive order, treating Bitcoin as a long-term reserve asset on par with gold. That July, he signed the GENIUS (Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins) Act, laying out regulatory guidelines for stablecoins.
Financial disclosures filed in June show he earned more than $1.4 billion from his crypto ventures. Over $500 million of it from World Liberty Financial, and another $635 million from sales of his $TRUMP meme coin. His reported income for the year was over $2.2 billion, much higher than his 2024 income of $600 million.
Founded in 2024, World Liberty Financial is at the heart of the Trump’s crypto empire. Its CEO Zach Witkoff, is the son of Mr. Trump’s West Asia envoy, Steve Witkoff. Other co-founders include Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Barron Trump, Steve Witkoff, and the President himself. This arrangement could blur the line that separates governance and private financial interests. The Trump administration sets policy, and the President’s family and allies benefit financially.
Mr. Tahnoon’s investment is especially notable given the UAE’s position as a key U.S. partner in West Asia. Since the beginning of the U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, Gulf countries have borne a significant share of Iran’s retaliatory attacks, with the war also disrupting maritime traffic in the region.
These relationships raise fundamental questions: Can a sitting President accept investments from a foreign government official in his companies?
Published - August 30, 2026 01:40 am IST

stories.headline: If any Hindu thinks there should be no Muslims in Bharat, he will not remain Hindu: Mohan Bhagwat
stories.bodyText: New York: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat on Saturday said if any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslims in Bharat, he will not remain a Hindu..The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) leader said this while addressing the One World: One Humanity Faith Leaders’ Summit..Bhagwat said that in Bharat, people of all denominations live. “By tradition, Bharat has given shelter to everybody. Those who could not find a safe place in the world came to Bharat, where they found their place,” he said..“We as RSS think, because we have this knowledge that world humanity is one, it is our duty to go all over the world and tell everybody that, in spite of diversities, we are one,” he said..“Muslim brothers asked me a question: You are a Hindu organisation, you see Hindu Rashtra, what about us Muslims? Would you drive us out? I said, no, that is not Hindutva. If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslims in Bharat, he will not remain Hindu,” he said..“Where there is ‘me’ and ‘mine’, there is no solution. ‘We’ and ‘ours’ is the solution,” he added..Many people and forces working against India's goal to become global leader: Mohan Bhagwat."We (RSS) are serving. While serving, we don’t see discrimination. Whoever is in need, we are serving. One lakh thirty thousand service projects are being run by our Swayamsevaks with the help of society. They served everywhere and served equally," Bhagwat said..Bhagwat arrived in the US on Tuesday as part of the RSS centenary-year global outreach programme. His outreach tour also includes Canada and the UK..In the US, he is scheduled to address a gathering of around 5,000 people at the iconic Madison Square Garden..In the US, Bhagwat has held meetings and discussions with members of the diaspora, Indian-American business executives and community leaders..The RSS chief also visited the Bhakti Centre in New York and also paid tributes to Indian spiritual leader Srila A C Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, founder of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON).

stories.headline: Police officer killed, another wounded in South Carolina park shooting; suspect dead
stories.bodyText:
Two people, including the suspect, and a police officer were killed, while another officer was wounded in a gunfight at a park in Columbia, South Carolina, the city’s police chief said Saturday (local time).
According to police, the incident began around 9:30 a.m. when a woman called authorities to report that a man against whom she had a restraining order was “destroying” property at her home.
Officer Christopher DeLong, who was later killed in the exchange of gunfire, arrived at the residence and learned that the suspect had already left. The woman provided DeLong with a description of the man and the vehicle he was believed to be driving.
At around 10:30 a.m., DeLong left the residence. Minutes later, after spotting a man near a vehicle matching the description provided by the woman, he radioed in a report of a suspicious person.
Officer David Dymock arrived as backup. Minutes later, Dymock radioed other officers saying that both officers “were hit and a suspect was down.”
Police identified the suspect as 33-year-old Adam Tyler Dowdy, who they said had a history of arrests in at least four states. 
Dowdy's previous charges included disorderly conduct, contempt of court, public intoxication, possession of a controlled substance and probation violations.
Who was officer Christopher DeLong
DeLong, 29, had served with the Columbia Police Department for two years before he was killed in the gunfight, Police Chief WH “Skip” Holbrook told reporters at a news conference.
He is survived by his wife and their two young children.
“Our hearts are broken this evening,” Holbrook remarked, becoming emotional at times. He urged officers to support one another through the tragedy, adding, “We will lean on each other in this tragic time. Let’s pray for this department.”
In a social media post, DeLong’s wife described the loss as “living a nightmare” and paid tribute to her husband as the “best dad to our babies.”
After the news conference, Holbrook and other law enforcement officials joined a procession from the hospital. Officer Dymock, who was wounded in the shooting, remained in stable condition.
The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division would investigate the shooting.

stories.headline: ‘ I take the blame myself’: Suryakumar Yadav’s big regret over failed ODI career
stories.deck: Suryakumar Yadav openly takes responsibility for his underwhelming ODI career, admitting he lacked the necessary dedication to the 50-over format. He struggles with the complexities of ODI cricket compared to T20s and expresses regret over not mastering the art of innings construction. Yadav reflects that his journey in ODI cricket feels incomplete and remains a lingering aspiration.
stories.bodyText:
Suryakumar Yadav
 has admitted that he only has himself to blame for failing to establish a longer career in ODI cricket, despite becoming one of India’s most successful T20 batters.
The former India T20I captain played 37 ODIs and scored 773 runs at an average of 25.76, numbers that never quite reflected the impact he had in the shortest format. His final ODI appearance came in the 2023 World Cup final against Australia, and he has not featured in India’s 50-over setup since.
Suryakumar, who led India to T20 World Cup glory earlier this year, acknowledged that his ODI career remains a source of disappointment. Rather than pointing to selection calls or circumstances, he accepted responsibility for not doing enough to adapt to the demands of the format.
“Hypothetically, we can say anything - that if I had come into the team in 2016, I could have played Tests and probably done well in ODIs too. But the reality is that I played only one Test and one innings. After that, the other players came back and started playing again, so it didn’t happen. But definitely, I am disappointed with myself when it comes to ODI cricket.
“It was a white-ball format, just like T20s, but to be very honest, I personally feel I did not put in as much effort as I should have for that format," Suryakumar Yadav said on 
Aakash Chopra
's YouTube channel.
Why Suryakumar found ODI cricket difficult
While T20 cricket has allowed Suryakumar to thrive with his aggressive strokeplay, he believes ODI cricket demands a far more calculated approach from batters.
He described the 50-over game as the most difficult format for a batter because situations can change rapidly, particularly for those coming in at No. 4, 5 or 6.
"I feel ODI cricket is probably the most difficult format to play as a batter, whether you are batting lower down the order or anywhere else. You can be two down for zero if you are batting at No. 4, or four down for 24 if you are batting at No. 6. Anything can happen. You have to bat almost like you do in a Test match. You see off the bowlers initially, give them respect and slowly build your innings. You may bat at a strike rate of 50 or sometimes 75, then take it to 100 and eventually finish at 130 or 140, much like you do in T20 cricket," he added.
According to Suryakumar, the challenge was not simply about batting in a different format. He struggled to work out exactly how he needed to construct an innings in ODI cricket, particularly in the middle order.
'I did not put in the extra effort'
Suryakumar revealed that he knew he was likely to occupy a middle-order role, but failed to put the same level of preparation into ODI cricket that he now gives T20 cricket.
“Personally, I feel I could not crack how to approach that format. I knew I was probably going to bat at No. 5 or 6, but even then, I did not work hard enough to understand the format. By the time I could blink, those 20-25 games had gone. I don’t even know when it happened or how it went by. 
And yes, I definitely regret not playing more ODI cricket. I wonder why I could not do better in that format. But no one is to blame. I take the blame myself because I did not put in the extra effort that I put in now when I play T20 cricket. If I bat for an hour, I will practise for an hour and a half," he said.
Suryakumar's ODI career therefore remains one of the unfinished chapters of his international journey. Despite making a major impact in T20 cricket, he could not translate that success into the 50-over format before his run in the ODI side came to an end after the 2023 World Cup final.

briefs.headline: Netanyahu condemns settler attack in flashpoint West Bank village
briefs.deck: President Isaac Herzog also condemned the attack in Qusra, while Israel's Foreign Ministry called the violence "a disgrace"
briefs.bodyText:
Dozens of Israeli settlers attacked the Palestinian village of Qusra in the northern occupied West Bank on Saturday (August 29, 2026) after nearly three weeks of tension in the area, drawing rare condemnation from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Earlier in August, a group of settlers began blocking supplies from entering Palestinian houses on the outskirts of the village near Nablus, trapping residents inside and drawing unusually strong criticism from the U.S. Ambassador.
Weeks later, Israeli forces continue to operate in the area while settlers still roam the surrounding hills.
On Saturday (August 29), Qusra residents and the military said dozens of settlers had descended on the village, throwing stones at residents and barricading themselves inside a house while Palestinians were inside.
In nearby Jalud, NBC News said masked settlers attacked and injured members of its reporting team and a Palestinian woman it had gone to interview.
"I strongly condemn the criminal acts of violence committed in the villages of Qusra and Jalud by a handful of rioters who are violating the law, causing a grave injustice to the law-abiding Jewish community, interfering with the IDF in carrying out its missions, and harming Israel's standing in the world," Mr. Netanyahu said in a statement.
President Isaac Herzog also condemned the attack in Qusra, while Israel's Foreign Ministry called the violence "a disgrace".
In Qusra, resident Yussef Abdul Kareem Hassan told AFP that a handful of villagers were doing work on a house on Saturday when they were approached by a small group of settlers.
The settlers then called for backup and returned with dozens more, Hassan said, adding that they surrounded the Palestinians inside the house and began throwing stones.
AFP footage of Qusra on Saturday showed dozens of Israeli forces deployed to the site.
Soaring violence
The Israeli military said soldiers and border police forces were dispatched "following reports that Israeli rioters had arrived in the area and that violent clashes had occurred, including stone-hurling toward Palestinians and additional civilians".
"Upon their arrival, the security forces identified dozens of rioters who had barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home while Palestinian residents were inside," the military said in a statement, adding that it was "aware of reports of Palestinian injuries".
It said forces had worked to remove the settlers from the house, separate the groups and confiscate vehicles "that were suspected of having been used to reach the area".
The vehicles would be used as evidence in a police investigation that has been opened, it said, adding that forces continued to operate in the area "to prevent further disturbances and restore order".
Violence by Israeli settlers towards Palestinians in the West Bank has persisted for years, often with little or no legal consequence, but recent months have seen a surge in attacks.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the Palestinian territory, which are illegal under international law, among some three million Palestinians.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967.
According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces or settlers have killed at least 1,103 Palestinians in the West Bank, including both militants and civilians, since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023.
Israeli figures show that at least 48 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period.
Published - August 30, 2026 02:40 am IST

briefs.headline: Ukraine's nuclear plant has lost power supply: IAEA
briefs.deck: The plant, which needs power to keep its six non-operating reactors cool, has only a ten-day diesel supply on site, the International Atomic Energy Agency said in a statement.
briefs.bodyText:
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in Ukraine has been without off-site power for more than a week and is currently relying on emergency diesel generators, the UN's nuclear watchdog said on Saturday (August 29, 2026).
The plant, which needs power to keep its six non-operating reactors cool, has only a ten-day diesel supply on site, the International Atomic Energy Agency said in a statement.
It has not had a delivery to an off-site storage facility in about six months, but the plant had been supplied with diesel Thursday and Friday from another off-site location, the IAEA added.
"The availability of diesel fuel is of paramount importance whenever a nuclear power plant loses off-site power," said IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi.
"The current situation once again shows why reliable external power and secure supply routes are indispensable for nuclear safety and security."
The plant lost its regular power supply "following military activity on the northern side of the Dnipro River", the statement said.
The Vienna-based group said it was trying to negotiate a local ceasefire to allow repairs to electrical lines.
On Friday, the IAEA said there had been three incidents this week involving drones at the Zaporizhzhia plant, injuring two employees, and raising renewed safety concerns.
The plant, in southern Ukraine, was seized by the Russian army in March 2022, just weeks after its full-scale invasion.
Both sides in the conflict regularly accuse the other of attacking the site on the banks of the Dnipro river that marks the frontline in the sector.
IAEA teams have had a permanent presence at the plant since September 2022. Zaporizhzhia's six reactors have been shut down since 2022.
Published - August 30, 2026 02:10 am IST

briefs.headline: Nepal flash floods updates: Rescuers claw through mud as death toll rises to 675
briefs.deck: Figures from Nepal and China put the number of missing people close to 3,000
briefs.bodyText:
Devastating flash floods in the Nepal-Tibet border region have killed at least 675 people, Nepali police said on Saturday (August 29, 2026). The Chinese state media earlier confirmed that seven were dead on the Tibetan side. Nearly 3,000 stranded people, including 163 foreigners, were evacuated by rescue teams in Nepal, as search and relief operations continued on the fourth day.
Nepal’s meteorology department has warned of fresh rainfall and thunderstorms in the flash flood-affected areas on Saturday, threatening to disrupt ongoing rescue and relief operations amid the worsening crisis, according to a media report. Meanwhile, Chinese authorities said the threat of a lake formed after a glacier collapse bursting near the Nepal-Tibet border has decreased. Satellite images from Thursday to Saturday morning suggest that water in the lake – straddling the border at the confluence of two rivers – has been slowly flowing through, decreasing the reservoir gradually, state broadcaster CCTV reported citing the Water Resources Ministry.
Also read | A shared disaster, beyond borders and geopolitics
According to the Nepal Army’s Public Relations Directorate, 2,465 people have been evacuated so far, including 163 foreigners — 113 Indians, 26 Chinese, 15 South Koreans, four Germans, two each from Italy and the U.S., and one Omani national. As many as 191 workers were evacuated from tunnels of various hydropower projects in Trishuli and Rasuwa, it said.
Editorial | Danger from above: On the Nepal flood
Nepal needs $4 billion to $5 billion for rebuilding after the devastating flood that struck its border areas this week, Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said. “This is just an estimate. Loss and damage is being assessed,” he said. More than ₹2.295 billion has been collected for the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund (PMDRF) by Friday night (August 29, 2026). The Ministry of Finance said the deposits were made to accounts held at 10 different commercial banks.
(With inputs from agencies)

briefs.headline: Another hooch tragedy in Gujarat exposes flaws in prohibition laws
briefs.deck: Another hooch tragedy exposes Gujarat’s legal inequality
briefs.bodyText: Ahmedabad: Another hooch tragedy struck “dry” Gujarat in mid-August, killing 13 people and leaving more than 60 others ill in the Bhavnagar district. They had liquor laced with toxic methanol.Investigation found that the liquor was consumed at an event celebrating a person’s selection in the Gujarat Police recruitment drive. The aspirant, who also fell ill after consuming the liquor, and others had bought it from a bootlegger — as is prevalent in the state.The other tragic aspect of the case was that the person who had come up with the formula for making the liquor using methanol also consumed the concoction and passed away.According to the police, the concoction was manufactured at a makeshift unit and bottled in containers bearing duplicate labels of a popular whisky brand. They were sold to consumers through a chain of bootleggers, exposing fault lines in the state government’s prohibition policy.A total of 27 suspects have been arrested in connection with the incident, which has once again highlighted how easily illicit liquor continues to be manufactured, distributed, and consumed in Gujarat, right under the nose of the police and administration.It has also put a big question mark over the implementation of the state’s liquor-prohibition policy, with alcohol flowing in from all its neighbours: Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Madhya Pradesh.State’s standAfter visiting those undergoing treatment following the Bhavnagar incident, Gujarat minister Jitu Vaghani was emphatic when he told reporters, "The state government's position on liquor prohibition policy is clear: There is no question of lifting prohibition… Not yesterday, not today and not tomorrow."The ground reality, however, is different. A little digging would reveal that his own government has, over the past three decades, gradually diluted the policy. As a result, it is considerably liberal in 2026.The government has created pockets where liquor can be legally sold and served in the garb of “ease of doing business” and promoting tourism. The latest tweak in the liquor regime was an exemption for GIFT City — the state government’s pet project where visitors from outside the state can eat and drink without the hassle of having to obtain a legal permit.Because of the policy shift, GIFT City — a global financial hub in the state capital of Gandhinagar — now has dedicated “beer bars” and wine-and-dine restaurants. The website of a prominent hotel even mentions “gourmet liquor”. It explains how “challenging” it was to find a bar in Gandhinagar, and that it now offers an “exclusive environment” where “business meets leisure” in a way that was previously prohibited in the state..In 2023, the Bhupendra Patel-led BJP government first announced relaxation in liquor prohibition laws for establishing wine-and-dine facilities in the GIFT City area, aimed at creating a "global business ecosystem" for "investors, technical experts, [and] national and international firms"..Gujarat hooch tragedy: 13 more arrested; 27 held so far.In 2025, the relaxation was further extended so outsiders — domestic or international — could consume liquor at designated hotels and restaurants simply by showing a photo identity card. They do not have to obtain a liquor permit..In June this year, the state government, through notifications, slashed value-added tax on foreign liquor served in GIFT City from 65% to 25%. The government also did away with the special fee of Rs 240 on a peg of 30-ml liquor serving. This was done to make pricing similar to other metro cities to create a "social life" that would attract talent from outside..Similar pockets have been created across the state where liquor laws are relaxed for visitors. On the other hand, laws for locals have only been becoming more stringent..Current situation.The prohibition has not been able to prevent hooch tragedies, which have struck Gujarat at regular intervals. Before Bhavnagar, the last major tragedy occurred in 2022, when 46 people died after consuming spurious liquor in the Botad and Ahmedabad districts. Before that, 156 people were killed in Ahmedabad in July 2009 after consuming illicit liquor, while many others lost their eyesight..In view of one of the worst tragedies, the Gujarat government introduced capital punishment for the illegal manufacture and sale of toxic alcohol, which became law in 2011. In 2017, the government increased the punishment for selling, consuming, and transporting illicit liquor to 10 years’ jail and a fine of Rs 5 lakh..While the law became stricter for locals, the state government has relaxed it for outsiders over the years. Visitors, barring those from dry states, can obtain liquor permits from authorised liquor stores based on their travel tickets..Former Gujarat deputy chief minister and influential Patidar leader Nitin Patel’s remarks to reporters were widely circulated after he admitted that the state was losing thousands of crores in revenue because of prohibition. However, he said the policy had helped maintain law and order..The government claims to have stringent laws that ensure a “complete” ban on liquor in the state, a policy Gujarat has followed since its inception in 1960, when it was carved out of the erstwhile Bombay state. While Maharashtra lifted prohibition, Gujarat retained it in the name of the values of Mahatma Gandhi, who was born in the state.

briefs.headline: The scrapping of Parandur airport project: a compilation
briefs.deck: This is a compilation of The Hindu’s coverage on the dropping of Parandur airport project by the TVK-led Tamil Nadu government in August 2026 citing farmers’ opposition and ecological concerns after the site was finalised during the DMK regime in 2022.
briefs.bodyText:
The Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK)-led Tamil Nadu government, fulfilling one of its poll promises, has officially announced that the proposed greenfield airport project planned as Chennai’s second airport at Parandur in Kancheepuram district would be dropped. Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay announced the decision in the Assembly on August 24, 2026 saying that Chennai needs a second airport, but not at the cost of agricultural land, farmers’ livelihoods.
The Parandur project, estimated to cost around ₹27,400 crore, was planned across 3,000 acres of fertile agricultural lands and was expected to eventually handle up to 100 million air passengers a year.
The move to drop the project four years after Parandur was finalised as the site for Chennai’s second airport comes in the backdrop of years of stiff opposition and sustained protests by the farmers and residents of villages around Ekanapuram in Kancheepuram district since 2022 who cited critical environmental threats; loss of farm lands, waterbodies and livelihoods; and risks of displacement of families.
On the other hand, the scrapping of the airport project has raised questions over the future course of action pertaining to the roughly 1,700 acres of agricultural lands that were already acquired during the tenure of the erstwhile DMK government.
Meanwhile, the chorus urging the State government to expedite the identification of an alternative, new site for Chennai’s second airport grows louder.

stories.headline: Karnataka High Court quashes SC/ST Act proceedings against 7 in property dispute
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Karnataka High Court has quashed criminal proceedings against seven persons from Anekal taluk, observing that the case amounted to an abuse of the process of law and that the dispute was essentially civil in nature.
The accused had been booked under Sections 3(1)(r), 3(1)(s), 3(1)(t), 3(1)(a) and 3(1)(za) of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, along with Sections 329, 351 and 45 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).
The complaint was filed by a woman identified as Uma. She alleged that the accused, including 
Manjunath
, had removed the tombstone of her late father from a property in Jigani and had abused her and her family members by referring to their caste.
The petitioners, however, contended that the property belonged to them and that a civil suit concerning the ownership of the property was already pending. Uma, on the other hand, claimed that the property was granted land.
Justice M Nagaprasanna, after examining the material on record, observed that the origin and substance of the dispute were “unmistakably shrouded in the colours of civil law.”
The court noted that a dispute that originated before the civil court and continued to be litigated there could not be transformed into a criminal case merely by adding allegations of criminality.
“Criminal law cannot be permitted to become a weapon of reprisal,” the judge observed, adding that it could not be used as a means to gain an advantage that a party had been unable to secure before the civil court.
The court further held that using criminal proceedings as a pressure tactic in an ongoing civil dispute constituted an abuse of the process of law.
Justice Nagaprasanna also observed that courts exercising jurisdiction under Section 528 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), corresponding to Section 482 of Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), must examine the circumstances surrounding a criminal complaint when there is a pre-existing civil dispute.
“When the chronology of events, pre-existing disputes between the parties and the attendant circumstances reveal that criminal proceedings are merely the latest weapon drawn from the armoury of a disgruntled litigant, it must look beyond the allegations and determine whether the prosecution is genuinely for a criminal offence or is being pursued for a purpose unrelated to criminal law,” the court observed.

stories.headline: Karnataka to seek drought relief from Centre
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru/Mysuru: 
Karnataka
 will submit a memorandum to the Centre seeking drought relief by the first week of Sept, deputy CM and revenue minister G Parameshwara said Saturday.
Parameshwara said govt had so far declared 101 taluks as drought-affected and will continue assessing the situation for another 15 days. More taluks could be added to the list based on the findings. Subsequently, central teams will visit the state to conduct a survey, following which drought relief will be released.
The Centre, he said, had decided to provide Rs 1,200 crore under State Disaster Response Fund and the state had sought its immediate release. “We will distribute the money to farmers within a week or 10 days,” he said, adding SDRF contribution will be shared between the state and Centre in 25:75 ratio.
Parameshwara said ensuring adequate drinking water, fodder for livestock and employment opportunities to prevent migration would be the govt’s immediate priorities. “We will decide on the compensation to be provided to farmers per acre. Drinking water, fodder for livestock and taking up works to prevent migration are our first priorities. We have already initiated measures in this regard,” he added.
Recalling the 2023 drought, Parameshwara said Karnataka had suffered losses estimated at Rs 39,000 crore and submitted a proposal seeking Rs 18,000 crore in relief. 
The state had to take the issue to the Supreme Court, following which Rs 3,500 crore was released.
Parameshwara said he had urged the Centre to avoid a repeat of the previous experience and immediately release funds under the State Disaster Response Fund.
The Centre, he said, had decided to provide Rs 1,200 crore under SDRF, and the state had sought its immediate release. “ I will help us provide compensation to farmers. We will distribute the money to farmers within a week or 10 days,” he said, adding that the SDRF contribution would be shared between the state and Centre in a 25:75 ratio.

stories.headline: South Korean machine tool player DN Solutions opens its first India plant in Bengaluru at an investment of ₹600 crore
stories.deck: Located in Bengaluru’s ITIR Industrial Area, the 25-acre facility is a strategic manufacturing, research and development, and service hub, and DN Solutions’ first overseas manufacturing investment since it established its Yantai facility in China in 2003
stories.bodyText:
South Korean machine tool manufacturer DN Solutions opened its first manufacturing facility in India in Bengaluru on August 26, 2026 at an investment of ₹600 crore. The facility was inaugurated by Karnataka’s Industries Minister M.B. Patil.
Located in Bengaluru’s ITIR Industrial Area, the 25-acre facility has been developed with the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB). The plant, a strategic manufacturing, research and development, and service hub, is DN Solutions’ first overseas manufacturing investment since it established its Yantai facility in China in 2003, according to company officials.
The company said the entire Phase 1 investment of ₹600 crore has been deployed already. It is also considering investments of a similar scale in future phases, depending on market demand and business growth.
The new facility would bring together manufacturing, R&D, a technical centre, after-sales service, training, and supply-chain development. Production would initially focus on the SVM series of vertical machining centres and LYNX and LEO horizontal turning centres, while the company plans to consider five-axis machine production in later phases.
“This is not a relocation of manufacturing from Korea or China. It is a completely new investment designed to create production capacity in India,” senior officials of DN Solutions told media persons.
In India for over 30 years
DN Solutions has been present in India for more than three decades, beginning sales operations in 1994. It established its Bengaluru Technical Centre in 2008 and its Indian subsidiary in 2016. The company said India’s expanding manufacturing base, engineering talent, young workforce, English-speaking population, and government initiatives such as Make in India make the country a key market for its long-term growth.
Karnataka, and Bengaluru in particular, was selected for its combination of precision manufacturing capabilities, engineering talent, automation expertise, and supply-chain infrastructure, it said.
Speaking at the inaugural, Wonjong Kim, CEO of DN Solutions said, “India clearly has the potential to become a global manufacturing powerhouse. Its large and expanding domestic market, English-speaking workforce, outstanding engineering talent, and young demographic profile are the foundations of its long-term competency. “
Kim also linked the company’s Bengaluru investment to the emergence of AI-enabled physical systems. “As AI expands beyond digital screens into the physical world, machines become indispensable. At the centre of that transformation phase are machine tools, serving as a core platform for Physical AI,” he explained.
Mr. Kim further said, “Bengaluru has a strong software ecosystem, which uniquely positions it to lead manufacturing in the Physical AI era. That is why we chose this City.”
Localisation at the centre of supply-chain strategy
The company plans to use the Bengaluru plant to build a more localised manufacturing ecosystem rather than moving existing suppliers from Korea or China to India. DN Solutions said it has already achieved around 80% localisation by parts count and aims to source most components domestically over the next five years, with spindle assemblies currently excluded from this target.
The company has already localised large-part machining, key machined components, and shaft-related parts in India. It is also working with local micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) on technical collaboration and capability development, with a formal supplier development programme planned for 2027.
“Our goal is to build a truly local manufacturing ecosystem that creates significant value within the country,” Kim added.
Focus on talent development
The Bengaluru facility is also expected to expand employment and skills development in India. DN Solutions currently employs 240 people directly in the country and plans to increase its direct workforce to 500. The broader employment impact across suppliers, logistics companies, and service providers is estimated to be at least twice the direct workforce.
Over the past year, the company has recruited around 100 recent graduates and operates a training centre and a one-year talent development programme. The company plans to work with customers, MSMEs, and educational institutions to develop application engineers, technicians, and machining specialists.
“Beginning with direct employment of 500 people, we intend to contribute to the development of a much larger talent pipeline through workforce training for customers and MSMEs, as well as partnerships with local educational institutions, “ Mr. Kim said.
DN Solutions ranks No. 1 in South Korea and No. 3 globally by revenue among machine tool manufacturers, according to the company. It has more than 140 sales networks, over 260 service networks, and 37 parts centres across 66 countries. The company has more than 450 machine models and says it has installed over 300,000 machines worldwide. Its portfolio also includes automation and digital manufacturing solutions.

stories.headline: Government sites to become EV charging hubs across Karnataka
stories.deck: Government departments have been directed to identify parking areas and vacant spaces on their premises that can be handed over for setting up the stations.
stories.bodyText:
Government offices and other public premises across Karnataka could soon double up as electric vehicle (EV) charging points, with the State planning to use its own land to expand the charging network under the Centre’s PM E-DRIVE scheme.
Gaurav Gupta, Additional Chief Secretary, Energy Department, has directed government departments to identify parking areas and vacant spaces on their premises that can be handed over for setting up the stations. The departments are required to submit the list to Bangalore Electricity Supply Company Limited (Bescom), the nodal agency for the scheme.
To make these stations accessible to the public around the clock, departments have also been asked to make separate entry and exit arrangements where necessary.
Of the 687 government locations surveyed by the Union Ministry of Heavy Industries, 515 have been approved in the first phase, while Bescom has proposed 1,250 charging stations in all, covering locations under 33 government departments.
There is also a financial incentive for departments that provide the land. Under the Union Power Ministry’s guidelines, the department that owns the land on which an EV station will come up will get a revenue share of ₹1 for every kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity consumed for charging. Bescom will sign a 10-year agreement with the department and take responsibility for setting up, running and maintaining the station.
The 1,250 proposed locations are divided into two categories: Category A includes Union and State government properties such as offices, hospitals, schools and college campuses, while Category B includes public facilities owned or managed by the government, such as railway stations, airports, metro stations and bus stations.
Bescom managing director N. Shivashankara said the utility had created a digital system to handle approvals, monitoring and subsidy-related work for the charging stations. The stations will also be linked to the EV Mitra platform, so users can find and access the charging points.
Four types of charging stations — fast chargers and normal chargers, have been proposed depending on whether they are located in cities or along highways. The proposed urban stations will require 133 sq. m. to 175 sq. m. of space, while highway stations will require between 221 sq. m. and 476 sq. m.

briefs.headline: Dug-up roads, dusty days: Bengaluru’s Shantinagar residents ask, when will it end?
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: For residents of central Bengaluru’s Shantinagar constituency, patience is wearing thin. Roads have been dug up for laying pipes, pavements are dotted with debris and clouds of dust have become part of daily life. Fed up with the prolonged disruption, residents are simply asking: When will these roads finally be restored?
Several key roads in the constituency, including Richmond Road, Langford Road, Lakshmi Road, parts of Hosur Road and Berlie Street, have been dug up over the past few months for a slew of underground infrastructure works, including water-supply pipelines and sanitary pipeline upgrades. Motorists and pedestrians are forced to weave through potholes, uneven surfaces, loose gravel and dust every day.
Residents say what was supposed to be a temporary disruption has begun to feel endless.
The problem is particularly acute on roads around busy educational institutions, including St Joseph’s University, where large numbers of students, pedestrians and motorists use the roads through the day. Students are increasingly being pushed onto the carriageway.
Langford Road has emerged as a major pain point. With traffic diverted or affected by ongoing Metro construction on Hosur Road, the road has seen increased vehicle movement. 
The unfinished stretches have only added to the chaos.
“Pavements are occupied by debris. Elderly people and schoolchildren are risking their lives as they are forced to walk on the road. Dust from the road is adding to vehicle emissions and causing health problems. Worse, honking has increased as vehicles jostle to stay on the unbroken stretch,” said a trader at Nanjappa Circle, questioning why the local MLA or BECC officials were not expediting the repair work.
The sentiment is echoed by Richmond Town residents, who ask why the roads cannot be restored immediately after pipe-laying is completed on each stretch. They also want to know how much longer they must wait for normal, dust-free roads.
Inset –1 (Haris mugshot)Wait for another three months, says MLA
MLA NA Haris defended the decision to postpone large-scale asphalting, saying the priority is to complete all pending underground utility works first so that newly laid roads do not have to be dug up again.
Once the works are completed, the roads will be fully restored and asphalted in a phased manner. A major project under way in Shantinagar is the expansion of the water-supply network. Of the 108 km of pipeline planned, around 68 km has been laid. Similarly, of the nearly 15,400 proposed house service connections, about 6,400 have been completed.
Haris said asphalting roads now would only lead to repeated digging by various agencies, wasting public funds and inconveniencing residents. “I understand the problems people are facing because of the ongoing road works. However, we have to bear this temporary discomfort to get durable road infrastructure. The idea is to complete all underground works in one go and then restore the roads. Once the roads are asphalted, no further cutting will be permitted unless absolutely necessary,” he said.

briefs.headline: No borders: Karnataka’s air quality partially choked by pollution from neighbouring states, finds study
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) and other local bodies across 
Karnataka
 may clean roads, tighten emission norms and curb local pollution, but there is no stopping cross-state air pollution. A recent study has highlighted the movement of pollutants across southern states and stressed that Karnataka’s worsening air quality cannot be tackled within political boundaries, as its cities receive a significant share of pollution from outside the state.
The study, by the Centre for Study of Science, Technology and Policy, titled Governance Framework for Airshed-Level Air Quality Management in South India, was released Wednesday at the India Clean Air Summit (ICAS) 2026 in Bengaluru. It called on Karnataka and its neighbouring southern states to adopt an airshed-based approach, under which multiple states jointly address pollution generated and transported across the region.
The study found that 47% of Karnataka’s annual average pollution originates within the South Indian region. Of this, 65% comes from sources within Karnataka and 35% from outside the state. Among the five southern states, Karnataka ranks third, after Kerala (65%) and Tamil Nadu (61%), and ahead of 
Andhra Pradesh
 (44%) and Telangana (38%).
Cross-state pollution accounts for 43% of Karnataka’s pollution during winter (Dec-Feb). Andhra Pradesh is the largest outside contributor, accounting for 15% of the pollution transported into Karnataka. However, the study found that Andhra Pradesh contributes relatively little to pollution levels in the other four southern states.
The findings assume significance as Bengaluru continues to grapple with rising pollution from multiple sources, while air quality is also deteriorating in several other parts of Karnataka. The study suggests that city-specific measures may not deliver sustained improvements if pollution generated in neighbouring states continues to reach Karnataka.
State’s central location
According to the report, Karnataka occupies a crucial position in South India’s pollution network because of its central geographical location. Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh are net contributors, exporting more pollution than they receive, while Kerala and Telangana are net receivers. Karnataka, meanwhile, both receives and exports moderate quantities of pollution.
Domestic activities, industries and open burning were identified as the three largest local sources of pollution across the five southern states. Domestic, energy and industrial sources were also identified as major contributors to transported particulate matter (PM2.5).
“In South India, the major gap in air quality management is the control of non-local pollution in these cities. The air quality over a particular city or state is not determined solely by sources located within its own boundaries but is also substantially influenced by upwind sources. A region can be upwind (a source of pollution) or downwind (a recipient of pollution) depending on geographical conditions and wind patterns. In South India, where transboundary pollution is substantial and varies by season, air quality action must shift from a city-level to an airshed-level approach,” the report highlighted.
Researchers explained that an airshed is a geographic area where pollutants are carried or accumulate, affecting air quality. “These are largely shaped by meteorology and topography rather than actual boundaries extending to several regions,” a researcher clarified.
What study suggests
The study has recommended creating an institution for South India, modelled on the Commission for Air Quality Management, to coordinate air pollution control across Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Kerala.
It has also called for a shift from city-specific projects to airshed-based pollution management. The five states have been recommended to develop a common pollution/emissions inventory to identify pollution sources and quantify the movement of pollutants across state boundaries. A common approved fuel framework and uniform targets for electric-vehicle adoption across the region are also suggested.

briefs.headline: Serbian model swaps ramp for garbage bag to clean Bengaluru’s streets
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 He came to India in 2018 for a modelling contract. Eight years later, Serbian model Lazar Jankovic has found a different way of giving back to the country he fell in love with — by picking up a garbage bag and cleaning its streets.
Lazar, 33, has spent six years in Bengaluru and two in Delhi, working mainly in modelling and commercials. Travelling across more than 20 states, however, exposed him to a problem he found difficult to ignore: garbage littering the streets. “The main problem is the trash on the street. And not just the trash, but the mindset regarding it,” said Lazar, who lives in Hennur.
After spending years understanding Indian culture, languages and the way people live, he started his ‘4cleanIndia’ campaign in Gurgaon in 2024. Even before that, he would carry a garbage bag and conduct small clean-ups wherever he travelled, from Rishikesh to Tamil Nadu to Sikkim.
He soon realised that cleaning a spot and posting a video was not enough. He turned his efforts into social-media challenges, encouraging others to clean their neighbourhoods. The initiative has since grown into a nationwide movement, with around 1.5 lakh people interacting with his social media page and sending messages and photographs of their own clean-up drives.
Lazar’s aim is not to clean every street in India, but to get people to take ownership of the spaces around them. “It’s about locals protecting their own thing,” he said.
In Bengaluru, he has cleaned around 10 spots, including Jayanagar, JP Nagar, Church Street and areas around Cubbon Park. About five have been documented through videos, while he continues smaller drives with local residents.
His strategy is to identify spots with a strong community and involve the residents. In Gurgaon’s Sector 55, for instance, residents formed WhatsApp groups and began monitoring areas after seeing Lazar clean their streets. “They saw a foreigner cleaning their streets and felt ashamed,” he said.
A similar response followed a recent drive near BDS Garden in Bengaluru. Garbage had accumulated again despite an earlier clean-up and warning posters. After Lazar cleaned the spot and posted a video clip, residents began taking responsibility for it. He said the area has remained clean for a month and a half since.
“I tell people ‘namma ooru, namma javabdari’ — it’s our city, so we need to protect it,” he said.
Lazar’s solution is simple: every household and shop should take responsibility for about two metres outside its premises
Lazar believes the problem is partly the result of how people view public spaces. Indians, he feels, are particular about keeping their homes clean but often do not extend that responsibility beyond their “chaar deewar” (four walls of their homes). “If my house is clean, if my things are sorted, then everything else is fine,” he said. “But if we take that psychology just a little bit outside to the streets, everything can change.”
His solution is simple: every household and shop should take responsibility for about two metres outside its premises. “Imagine if this happens as a nationwide movement where everyone, every Sunday, goes outside and cleans this much. Half the problem is gone,” he said.
Lazar also believes cleanliness campaigns need less “gyaan” and more emotion. “India runs on chai and emotion,” he said, arguing that lectures about saving the planet or cleanliness are unlikely to change behaviour. “Nobody cares,” he said, adding that celebrities and other influential figures should instead make cleanliness a trend through music and videos. His philosophy is to make it “fun”, “dance-worthy” and entertaining rather than another lecture on civic responsibility.
Lazar is also seeking govt participation. He has been in touch with the office of Shivajinagar MLA Rizwan Arshad about a larger clean-up initiative in the constituency and hopes to collaborate with govt representatives.

briefs.headline: Gallery Sumukha at 30: How Premilla Baid shaped Bengaluru’s art scene
briefs.deck: From a shared space next to a doctor’s clinic in Wilson Garden to a 30-year legacy, Gallery Sumukha reflects Bengaluru’s distinct, entrepreneurial spirit
briefs.bodyText:
Quite often, patients from the neuro clinic that shares its premises with Gallery Sumukha walk into the gallery’s cavernous front room, filled with paintings and sculptures without knowing what the space is for. Premilla Baid, 73, the founder of the gallery which marks its 30th anniversary this month, finds these serendipitous drop-ins the best way for people to engage with art. The gallery doesn’t seem incongruous in a mixed-use building, with a doctor’s chamber and clinic out front. The doctor has been her generous landlord for decades.
The neighbourhood it’s located in, though close to the city’s central business district, isn’t the typical upmarket area one associates with sumptuous art galleries. And yet, Wilson Garden has been growing into an art and culture hub with such spaces as 1 Shanthiroad, The Courtyard, and the Attakalari Centre for Movement Arts. This defines Bengaluru’s art ecosystem in contrast to its arguably more sophisticated counterparts, Delhi and Mumbai — it is unpretentious, understated and a little scrappy.
Founded in 1996, Gallery Sumukha first started from Baid’s home, then shifted to the Alliance Francaise building before relocating to its current location in 1999. Today, spread over 5,000 sq.ft., Sumukha is housed in the largest private gallery space in South India. Designed by architect Vikram Sardesai, it was built to accommodate large-scale installations, sculptures, and multimedia showcases that smaller commercial galleries of south could not host.
A gallery is born
Moving back to India after six years in Ireland, Baid was deeply inspired by art doyenne Sara Abraham’s Kala Yatra. Self-taught Baid held her first exhibition for a charitable organisation at the Oberoi Hotel. “In those days [1996], we sold paintings worth about ₹5 lakh. That was a lot of money. Then it got into me,” she says. “I don’t know a word of art in the technical sense, I started the gallery out of pure passion alongside my medical practice.”
Baid is careful not to call herself a curator but a gallerist. “Curators usually have technical training and an educational background in art. I just put shows together, relying on my judgment and understanding gained over three decades,” she says. Initially funded by her own savings, the gallery has always been self-sustained. “Whatever money we make goes back into the gallery. Participating in art fairs is expensive. We may make some money here, go to an international art fair, and return without having sold anything, so it’s difficult to turn a profit,” she says. Baid chose sustainability over aggressive commercial growth. The gallery’s entry into Chennai, at her parents’ home, in 2006, lasted around six years.
The early days
Until the 1970s, Bengaluru didn’t play a prominent role in India’s art world, says artist-sculptor Balan Nambiar, 88. “Karnataka Chitrakala Parishath held annual ‘all-India’ art exhibitions with works by regional artists… displayed at the banquet hall of Vidhana Soudha. In the 70s, Bengaluru had only two freelance artists: Rumale Chennabasavaiah and myself. Most others were employed in government institutions,” he says.
At the time, Kritika Gallery on St. Marks Road, run by Kausalya Dayaram, was, Nambiar recalls, the city’s only private art gallery, while Kala Yatra made a big impact in its brief existence. “Many galleries (Sakshi Gallery; Gallery SKE) later appeared and disappeared within short spans,” adds the artist who’s been a regular at the gallery since the beginning.
Amid government-owned (Venkatappa Art Gallery) and commercial art spaces (Krithika Art Gallery; Kala Yatra), Sumukha quickly garnered the reputation of being among the first ‘serious’ art galleries in Bengaluru’s then-nascent art world in the 1990s. The 2000s-10s saw the gallery grow into a major commercial contemporary-art space and expand its international art-fair presence.
Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, chairperson of Biocon and a prominent art collector says, “Gallery Sumukha elevated the level of art galleries in Bengaluru. Before it came along, most galleries would be a bit of everything, from professional to amateur stuff. Premilla paid attention to the market, she organised events around artists and brought in a certain level of professionalism in curation that was missing from the art space in the city.”
Rallying behind artists
Sumukha wasn’t conceived simply as a place to sell paintings; Baid has been using it as a space for workshops (printmaking; sculpture), lectures and experiments. Artist Pushpamala N. says, “Sumukha has been encouraging new and experimental work and has been host to all our works in different media, installations and live performances. It has hosted talks and book releases. And recently, walkthroughs during those exhibitions attended by large groups of school students and art students. This major art space is on the bucket list of every visiting curator and artist.”
Over three decades, Gallery Sumukha has mounted an estimated 230 shows, and worked with 100-plus artists. Its roster has included veteran Bengaluru-based artists such as Yusuf Arakkal and S.G. Vasudev to Vadodara-based Gulammohammed Sheikh, whose book of art prints was recently published by Sumukha, and K. Laxma Goud, as well as major contemporary figures such as Atul Dodiya, Pushpamala N., G. Ravinder Reddy and Paresh Maity. City artist Ravikumar Kashi, whose career has explored the versatility of paper as a medium, has been nurtured by Sumukha since the ‘90s.
Crucial to the gallery’s continued relevance has been its work with artists who have drawn critical and commercial attention globally — veterans like Gulammohammed Sheikh to mid-career artists like Paresh Maity. The association with Maity in the South was crucial to Sumukha’s own success. Baid, who’s taken Maity to many international art shows, calls him the gallery’s biggest “saviour”.
One of the biggest success stories of the gallery is Shivaraju B.S. aka Cop Shiva, a former policeman turned internationally recognised artist and photographer. “She [Baid] gave me my first solo show in 2012. You can say she found me — I was working as a coordinator at 1 Shanthiroad at the time and a friend asked me to meet her with my work,” says Shiva. The rest, as they say, is history.
The road ahead
Bengaluru today has a much more flourishing art scene than it did when Sumukha was founded. Although the city is one of the three major hubs of the Indian art market, its IT wealth doesn’t convert to art sales, which are a minor proportion of the overall sales in the country, especially when compared to the more mature markets of Mumbai and Delhi. “It is changing, but historically, there are two aspects to this: One, Bengaluru is a much younger city and the wealth is more recent… conspicuous consumption is much more in Delhi and Mumbai compared to Bengaluru, and the proliferation of galleries is less in the South compared to the North. The other factor is the growth of [geography-agnostic] online art sales,” says Abhishek Poddar, Founder-Trustee of Museum of Art & Photography (MAP) and a prominent figure in the city’s cultural space.
The gallery is marking its three decades with a rare solo show of Reddy’s sculptures. “We don’t do e-commerce, we don’t think very far ahead in terms of technology, AI art, that sort of thing. I stick to what I know best — finding good artists, young artists. I want to do better shows — that’s it,” says Baid.
The writer is an independent journalist based in Bengaluru.

briefs.headline: Garbage dumping in Bengaluru’s lakes turns fatal for Indian darters
briefs.deck: Birders and animal rescuers are noticing a sharp increase in the number of birds in distress at the city’s many lakes
briefs.bodyText:
Renuka Selvamani, a birder and bird photographer, has noticed a strange phenomenon at her regular haunt, Doddanekundi Lake. “I am seeing more cases of birds in distress,” she says, pointing out that the culprit is trash dumped by humans. The Oriental or Indian darter (Anhinga melanogaster), also known as the snakebird, a tropical water bird with a long, slender neck and a sharp, spear-like beak that it uses to impale fish, seems to be afflicted more than others, Renuka says.
“The darters are very sensitive because of their beaks, which get entangled in waste, such as the net used to pack onions,” explains Renuka, who works as a data scientist with the Expedia Group. She adds that when this happens, they cannot hunt or feed themselves, and end up starving to death. “I have seen three birds whose beaks have been tied like this,” she says.
And this is not happening only at Doddanekundi Lake. According to Jayanthi Kallam, the Executive Director of the Avian and Reptile Rehabilitation Centre (ARRC) in Horamavu, there is a surge in the number of darters in distress reported from at least 10 lakes in the city. She points out that there have been sightings at lakes like Doddanekundi, Jakkur, Yelahanka, Rachenahalli, Hesarghatta, Sampengahalli, Lalbagh and Chelkere, among others.
While the issue itself is not a new one — the darters’ pointed beaks, adapted to spear fish, have always been vulnerable to the large quantities of garbage regularly dumped in the city’s water bodies — the number of birds in distress that have been spotted has gone up considerably this year, says Jayanthi. “We would get a couple of birds every year. But this year we are seeing a sudden surge in the numbers,” she says, adding that ARRC now sees at least one case every week. “Also, a lot of bird watching groups and lake groups are reporting more and more sightings.”
Certain types of garbage seem to be causing most of the danger, says Jayanthi: plastic wrappers or bags, discarded fishing nets and puja items. “People who discard puja cloth don’t even realise the dangers of it, but these tiny pieces of cloth, bright in colour, end up attracting the birds,” she says. Their beaks get tangled in these bits of cloth, and they can’t remove them. “Unlike some birds, like raptors, for instance, who can lift their legs and clean their beak, darters are not built like that. They will wiggle and shake their head, but it is very difficult for them to get something out once it is stuck.”
Additionally, since they are flighted birds, rescuing them also becomes difficult. “We have a team dedicated to this…use a motorised boat, drone tracking and binoculars. But because these are flighted birds, if you intervene too soon, they simply go away.” While they have rescued some birds, they would be in an extremely weak and emaciated condition by the time they are rescued, says Jayanthi.
Some birdwatchers are now planning a poster campaign to raise awareness about the issue. “I am still in talks with local nature groups and trying to figure out permissions,” says Praveen, an avid birder from the city. As someone who has seen several dead birds and spoken to other birders who have also noticed this trend, he believes it is important to educate people about the pressing issue. “We are trying to set up awareness posters highlighting the problem, possible cause and solution,” he says

stories.headline: Passed over in 2020, Bharucha likely to succeed Jagadishan
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Sashidhar Jagdishan’s decision not to seek another term has brought Kaizad Bharucha, an 
HDFC Bank
 old guard and an earlier contender for the top job, into focus as a possible successor.
Sources said a successor will be in place before Jagdishan steps down in Oct, but the process will take time as RBI will need to clear the appointment. Bharucha, an executive director at HDFC Bank, was among those considered for CEO position when Jagdishan was selected to succeed Aditya Puri in 2020. His association with the bank and his elevation to executive director rank make him one of the prominent internal candidates.
The bank is understood to have been preparing for the succession process, with Jagdishan himself until recently seen as a candidate for another term. RBI typically seeks multiple names before approving the appointment of a private-bank CEO.
K Balasubramanian, CEO of Citi India and a former head of corporate banking at HDFC Bank, is seen by some in the industry as a potential candidate. Hitendra Dave, CEO of HSBC India, is another possible name given his experience running a large multinational bank in India.
The choice of an internal candidate such as Bharucha would provide continuity at a bank that has undergone considerable change since Puri’s departure. But the old guard has steadily thinned out. Several of the senior executives promoted under Puri have left the bank in recent years.
Arvind Kapil, who headed the group’s retail business, left in April 2024. CHRO Vinay Razdan left in June 2025, followed by group head Parag Rao in September 2025 and retail head Rahul Shukla in October 2025. Executive director Bhavesh Zaveri was the latest senior departure, leaving the bank in April 2026. The exits have left Bharucha as one of the more prominent senior bankers from the Puri era at HDFC Bank. His candidacy could therefore assume greater significance as HDFC moves to find a successor.
After a period marked by the HDFC merger, technology-related problems and a series of governance controversies, brokers have called for greater clarity on succession to help steady the bank and reduce uncertainty.

stories.headline: Union, Canara Bank to appeal NCLT's Chandra order
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Canara Bank and Union Bank of India are challenging NCLT's approval of Zee group founder Subhash Chandra's repayment plan, under which creditors would recover 0.03% of their admitted claims relating to his liabilities as a personal guarantor, arguing that the plan was approved despite opposition from public-sector creditors.
The insolvency proceedings were initiated by Indiabulls Housing Finance against Chandra. Canara Bank, which has a 1.6% voting share, and Union Bank of India, which has 0.76%, opposed the repayment plan and sought its rejection. LIC Housing Finance, with a 6.1% voting share, also voted against the plan. However, the plan secured the support of private creditors holding an 80.8% voting share and was approved by NCLT.
The total admitted claims stood at Rs 22,006 crore, of which Rs 6.5 crore was proposed to be paid, including Rs 6.3 crore to creditors and Rs 25 lakh towards process costs. This amounts to a 99.9% haircut, with creditors recovering about 0.03% of their admitted claims.
Canara Bank has said it sought a forensic audit, but the request could not be pursued because of its minority voting share. The bank is therefore challenging National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) order before National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT).
On Thursday, HDFC Bank confirmed that it plans to appeal NCLT order before NCLAT. Its claim of Rs 697.59 crore accounted for about 3.17%, or 3.2%, of the total admitted claims.
Zee group founder Subhash Chandra has disputed the Rs 22,000 crore liability, saying it reflected historical claims filed in 2022. He put the claims of objecting creditors at Rs 3,992 crore, of which Rs 620 crore had been settled, while borrowing entities had offered another Rs 1,063-1,113 crore. The remaining Rs 16,201 crore of claims by creditors who supported the plan were also being addressed by the principal borrowers. Chandra said he was only a personal guarantor and had not himself borrowed the money.
Lenders are also not satisfied with the finding that Chandra had only about Rs 6 crore in personal assets, particularly since his house was also mortgaged. Union Bank of India (UK) has similarly said it rejected the resolution plan and argued before NCLT that it should not be approved. It is now challenging NCLT’s decision before the NCLAT.

stories.headline: No material price impact on CBG with revised offtake framework, ensures plants operate sustainably: Govt.
stories.deck: The Union Petroleum Ministry stated that the government funded support would translate to only a 28% increase in price of CBG offtake.
stories.bodyText:
Addressing concerns about compressed biogas (CBG) becoming increasingly expensive with the revised offtake price, the Union Petroleum Ministry assured the pricing cushioned with government-funded support and stacking with a substantially wider gas pool would avert any material price impact.
The Union Cabinet August 6 approved the GOBARdhan scheme that introduced CBG offtake price of ₹2,110 per metric million British thermal unit (MMBTU).
Responding to a media report, it added that the revised pricing framework seeks to provide CBG producers with a “stable and viable” price that would enable them to operate “sustainably”.
The ministry clarified that full offtake price would not be recovered through gas consumers.
It explained that the government would provide an affordability cushion of ₹10 per kilogram of CBG – which equates to about ₹215 per MMBtu of CBG with 95% methane content.
Effectively, with the financial support, the cost of CBG would stand at ₹1,895 per MMBtu.
This would be approximately 28% higher than the prevailing price of ₹1,478 per MMBtu.
The Petroleum Ministry also argued that CBG is not sold at the procurement price to city-gas distributors. It is pooled with other domestically produced natural gas, and the cost is spread based on the proportionality in the domestic gas pool.
Previously, the cost of CBG was spread across a limited quantity of the administered price-mechanism gas allocated to the CNG (transport) and PNG (Domestic) segments.
“Under the new framework, the net cost of CBG will be spread across a domestic gas base approximately 2.5 to 3 times larger than the earlier base,” it stated, adding, “Due to the spreading of CBG cost on a much larger gas pool, the price impact on an individual gas consumer will be negligible.”

stories.headline: Ather unveils new bike Konarc, new battery platform, charging solution for apartments

Ather Energy, Bengaluru-based electric two-wheeler manufacturers, on Saturday announced Konarc, Ather’s newest scooter; Ather True Health, a comprehensive vehicle health report and resale-value assessment; the fifth-generation Ather Bedrock Battery platform; and Ather Node, a charging solution for apartment communities.
Together, these announcements are expected to address key barriers consumers continue to face with electric two-wheelers, from everyday usability and battery safety to long-term battery health, resale value and access to convenient home charging, according to the EV firm.
Konarc, the first product built on Ather’s new EL platform, is targeted at mainstream Indian riders, focusing on ride comfort, stability, everyday usability, and serviceability. Konarc is available in six variants across the S and Z product lines, with IDC (Indian Druiving Cycle) range options from 100 km to 200 km. All variants come with the fifth-generation Bedrock Battery and a 10-year/1,00,000 km (whichever is earlier) warranty with a 70% state-of-health guarantee.
Tarun Mehta, Co-Founder & CEO, Ather Energy, said, “This year, we have some of our biggest launches across the vehicle, battery, charging and ownership experience. Each of these comes from a different problem we have been working on, but the larger goal is the same: to keep removing the barriers that come with new technology and make EVs a more natural choice for more people.’’
According to Ather, Bedrock Battery platform offers BreachSense, a real-time monitoring system designed to detect microscopic damage following a high-impact accident. With this, Ather expects batteries to reach 70% state of health much later at approximately 1L to 1.2L KMs, compared to around 80,000 to 1,00,000 km for the previous generation.
AtherNode is a charging solution designed to address one of the key challenges of charging electric 2Ws and 4Ws in residential and commercial spaces with limited available load.
